interview_metadata.name: Sean Buckley
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Dubuque, Iowa, in 1976, and grew up in a working-class Irish-American family where you learned early to show up on time, fix what you could fix, and not make a big production out of yourself. My dad worked maintenance at a manufacturing plant, and my mom was a clerk at a local credit union, so money was steady but never loose. I was a quiet kid, more comfortable taking apart radios or building model kits than being the loud one at school. In high school I got interested in computers through a math teacher who let a few of us stay after school and use the lab, and that was the first place where my tendency to be patient and detail-oriented felt like an advantage. I went to community college and earned an associate degree in computer information systems, then started doing support work before moving into programming. I met my wife, Megan, in my late twenties when I was working in Colorado, and we eventually moved to Livingston, Montana, because we wanted a smaller place with access to mountains, rivers, and a real community. We have two kids, Claire and Owen, and most of my adult life has been balancing software work, family, and getting outside whenever I can. The biggest themes for me have been steady work, building reliable things, and trying not to let a career in technology pull me away from the outdoors and family.

follow_ups.question: What was a typical day like for you as a kid in Dubuque?
follow_ups.response: School, chores, dinner at home, and then either homework or tinkering in the basement. On weekends I helped my dad with yard work or small repairs, and Sundays were usually family meals after church when I was younger.

follow_ups.question: When did you first feel like software might become your career?
follow_ups.response: Probably around my second year at community college. I wrote a little inventory program for a class project, and I liked that if you were careful, you could make something useful and repeatable.

follow_ups.question: What brought you specifically to Livingston?
follow_ups.response: We had visited Yellowstone and the Paradise Valley a few times, and Livingston felt practical rather than resort-like. It had enough work within reach, especially with remote options, but it still felt like a town where people know each other.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was leaving a comfortable job in Denver and moving to Montana. At the time I was working for a mid-sized software company, doing decent work, but I was spending more time in traffic and meetings than with my family or outside. Megan and I had young kids then, and we started asking whether more salary was really buying us the life we wanted. I found a software position that paid less but allowed some remote work and had an office connection in Bozeman, so we took the leap. It was stressful because we had to sell a house, find schools, and accept a tighter budget. But it changed the rhythm of my life. I became more intentional about work, got involved at the library teaching basic computer skills, joined the Livingston Outdoor Recreation Club, and started seeing my career as something that should support a full life instead of swallowing it.

follow_ups.question: What made the decision feel risky at the time?
follow_ups.response: Mostly the money and stability. I was giving up a clear career ladder in Denver for a smaller market where there were fewer backup options if the job went sideways.

follow_ups.question: How did Megan feel about the move?
follow_ups.response: She was nervous but on board. She liked the idea of a slower pace and better access to trails, but she was the one reminding me we still had kids, a mortgage, and health insurance to think about.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was definitely a conscious choice. I had spreadsheets for the budget, school options, commute times, even what winter utilities might look like in Livingston.

follow_ups.question: Did that planning make you feel more confident?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but only to a point. Planning told me the move was possible; it did not remove the uncertainty.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to before deciding?
follow_ups.response: Megan first, then my brother Patrick and a former manager who had gone remote before it was common.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A relocation stipend or better remote-work guidance would have helped. We figured out a lot ourselves, from health insurance timing to school enrollment.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help informally?
follow_ups.response: A coworker in Bozeman gave me honest advice about the local tech scene, and that mattered.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would you offer someone making a similar move?
follow_ups.response: I would tell them to budget conservatively, visit in the off-season, and talk to locals before romanticizing the place.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Megan, and we have been married for twenty-two years. She works part time doing bookkeeping and office work for a local outfitter, and she is the more socially tuned-in one between the two of us. Our daughter Claire is twenty-one and at Montana State in Bozeman studying environmental science, so she is not home full time but comes back for weekends, laundry, and family dinners. Our son Owen is seventeen and still at home; he is into robotics, cross-country, and guitar, so there is usually some project or practice schedule on the fridge. My brother Patrick is still in Iowa, and we talk every couple of weeks, mostly about family, work, and the Broncos if they are doing badly enough to complain about. My parents are both retired and still in Iowa, though my dad has slowed down physically. Family for me is not flashy. It is checking in, showing up, splitting chores, and making sure Sunday dinner happens when everyone is around.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Megan usually do together during the week?
follow_ups.response: Most weeknights we cook dinner, walk around the neighborhood if the weather is decent, and read or watch one episode of something before bed.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Claire now that she is in Bozeman?
follow_ups.response: Usually twice a month in person, more if there is a birthday or she wants to hike. We text several times a week.

follow_ups.question: What is your relationship with Owen like day to day?
follow_ups.response: Pretty good. We connect through practical things, like helping him debug a robotics issue or driving him to meets, rather than long heart-to-heart talks every night.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My parents, Tom and Eileen Buckley, are important to me. They are in their late seventies in Iowa, and I call them every Sunday evening.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit them often?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a year, sometimes twice if there is a family event or health concern.

follow_ups.question: What are those calls usually about?
follow_ups.response: Health, weather, what the kids are doing, and whatever small repair my dad is trying to talk through.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small circle rather than a big one. My closest local friends are Dave, who I fly fish with on the Yellowstone, and Linda and Mark, a couple we know through the outdoor club. I also stay connected with two coworkers, Priya and Nate, because we have worked through enough difficult releases together that the trust is real. Once a month I volunteer at the library teaching basic computer skills, and I would not call every person there a close friend, but that group gives me a sense of belonging. I am not someone who needs a full calendar of social events. A good Saturday with one friend on the river is more my speed.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Dave?
follow_ups.response: In summer, probably every other Saturday morning if the river conditions are good. In winter it is more coffee or a beer once a month.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually meet friends?
follow_ups.response: At the trailhead, the river access, the library, or occasionally at Neptune's or Katabatic for a beer.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Livingston, Montana, in a modest residential neighborhood with older houses, cottonwoods, garages that double as workshops, and people who still wave when they walk by. It is not fancy, but it is close enough to downtown that I can get to the library, hardware store, and a couple of coffee shops in a few minutes. The Yellowstone River is nearby, and the mountains are always part of the backdrop. You get a mix of longtime residents, people connected to outdoor work, retirees, and more remote workers than there used to be. Winters can be hard with wind and ice, but there is a real neighborly quality. If someone's fence comes down or a car will not start, people notice.

follow_ups.question: Who do you know best nearby?
follow_ups.response: Our next-door neighbor, Walt, is a retired electrician. We trade tools sometimes, and I shovel his walk if the snow gets heavy.

follow_ups.question: What places do you use most in town?
follow_ups.response: The public library, the hardware store, the grocery, local breweries, and the river access points.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe here. We lock our doors and do the normal things, but I am comfortable walking in the evening or letting Owen bike to a friend's house.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Mostly minor stuff, like unlocked cars getting rummaged through a few years ago.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, informally. People notice unfamiliar cars or if someone has not been seen for a few days.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is the access to nature and the sense of community. The downside is rising housing costs, winter weather, and fewer specialized services than you would have in a bigger city.

follow_ups.question: What cost increase do you notice most?
follow_ups.response: Property taxes and groceries. Also contractors are expensive because everyone is busy.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there despite that?
follow_ups.response: The river, the mountains, our friends, and the fact that it still feels like a place where our habits fit.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, Megan, and our son Owen living in the house full time. Claire is at Montana State, so she is home on some weekends and breaks but not counted as living here day to day. We do not have anyone staying temporarily right now. The house runs on a pretty ordinary rhythm: I work mostly from a small office, Megan works part time, and Owen's schedule shifts with school, robotics, and running.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household chores?
follow_ups.response: Megan handles a lot of scheduling and bills, I do cooking several nights and repairs, and Owen has dishes, trash, and lawn mowing in summer.

follow_ups.question: Does your work-from-home setup affect the household?
follow_ups.response: A bit. Everyone knows if my office door is closed during core hours, I am probably in a meeting or deep in code.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone currently in the household is permanent.

follow_ups.question: Does Claire count as temporary when she visits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she visits but lives mainly in Bozeman during the school year.

follow_ups.question: Do relatives ever stay for long stretches?
follow_ups.response: No, usually just a few days at a time.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Claire stays during breaks, and my parents or Megan's sister might visit for a few days.

follow_ups.question: Where do guests usually sleep?
follow_ups.response: In Claire's room if she is away, or on the pullout in the basement family room.

follow_ups.question: How often do you host visitors?
follow_ups.response: Maybe four or five times a year.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: Claire is away at school in Bozeman, but otherwise no.

follow_ups.question: Is she home during summers?
follow_ups.response: Part of the summer, though she may take fieldwork or a seasonal job.

follow_ups.question: Anyone away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am usually up around 6:15, make coffee, check the weather, and read a little news before work. I start work around 8:00, with meetings clustered mid-morning and coding or reviews in the afternoon. Tuesdays and Thursdays I try to walk or do a short run after work, and Wednesdays I often help Owen with robotics or drive him somewhere. Megan and I cook most nights, usually something simple unless it is the weekend. Once a month I volunteer at the library in the evening. Saturdays vary by season: fishing or hiking in summer, cross-country skiing in winter, and woodworking if the weather is ugly.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:30 on weeknights, maybe 11:00 if I am reading a good novel.

follow_ups.question: What is your most predictable weekly routine?
follow_ups.response: Coffee at 6:30, work by 8:00, dinner around 6:30. I like those anchors.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a senior software developer for a regional software firm that serves logistics, inventory, and small business clients. My stack is mostly Java, C#, Python, SQL, and some Angular when needed, though I am more backend and systems-oriented than front-end. I work Monday through Friday, generally 8:00 to 5:00, mostly from home with one or two days a month in Bozeman for planning sessions. A normal day includes code reviews, writing or refactoring services, database work, documentation, and mentoring younger developers. We use Agile, though I am the person who keeps asking whether the ticket is actually clear enough to build.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you enjoy most?
follow_ups.response: Designing something that is boring in the best way, meaning it runs reliably and nobody has to think about it.

follow_ups.question: What part is most frustrating?
follow_ups.response: Unclear requirements and rushed timelines. Most defects start before anyone writes code.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I maintain the garden, handle most of the home repairs, and do the heavier snow shoveling. I also keep a pretty detailed budget spreadsheet, because that is just how my brain works. On Sunday evenings I call my parents and usually prep lunches or ingredients for the week. I try to spend a couple hours a week studying AWS architecture material because I want that certification. And then there is the model railroad in the basement, which sounds like a toy, but I treat it like a long-running engineering project.

follow_ups.question: What do you grow in the garden?
follow_ups.response: Potatoes, carrots, onions, kale, tomatoes if the season cooperates, and herbs like rosemary and thyme.

follow_ups.question: When do you study for AWS certification?
follow_ups.response: Usually early Saturday morning or one weeknight after dinner, about two to three hours total.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is Owen being busier with school and activities, so evenings have more driving and coordination than they used to. Work has also shifted toward more architecture planning, which means fewer uninterrupted coding blocks and more design reviews. I have been trying to protect Friday afternoons for documentation and cleanup work, because otherwise technical debt piles up. Health-wise, I added more lunchtime walks after my doctor warned me about borderline blood pressure. It is not dramatic, but it changes the shape of the day.

follow_ups.question: How consistent are the lunchtime walks?
follow_ups.response: Three days a week when the weather is reasonable. In winter I sometimes use a basic treadmill in the basement.

follow_ups.question: Do you like the architecture planning work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly. It is the direction I want to go, but it requires patience with meetings.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Owen is the one still on a school-year routine at home. He is up around 6:45, eats something quick, and either drives himself or gets a ride depending on the day. After school he has cross-country in the fall, robotics club in winter, and occasional guitar lessons. He does homework at the kitchen table or in his room, and if he gets stuck on math or coding, he will ask me after dinner. Claire's college routine is her own now, though she has labs, field days, and part-time work when she can get it.

follow_ups.question: Who usually handles transportation for Owen?
follow_ups.response: He handles some of it now, but Megan and I still split pickups when weather is bad or schedules collide.

follow_ups.question: Do you attend his activities?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially meets and robotics showcases. I try not to hover, but I show up.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been pretty limited and mostly routine. I have had a couple of speeding tickets over the years, including one on I-90 when I was trying to get to Bozeman too quickly. In Livingston, I see local police at community events or around downtown, but I do not have regular interactions. I know my experience is shaped by being a middle-aged white guy in a small town, so I generally get the benefit of the doubt. I try to keep that in mind when people describe different experiences.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called law enforcement yourself?
follow_ups.response: Once for a minor fender bender and once when a neighbor's garage door was open late at night and they were out of town.

follow_ups.question: How were those interactions?
follow_ups.response: Professional and uneventful.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A search-and-rescue briefing after a hiker went missing near a trailhead stands out. It was a reminder that law enforcement here is often tied into outdoor safety too.

follow_ups.question: Were you involved in the search?
follow_ups.response: Not directly. Our outdoor club helped share information and later discussed preparedness.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your outdoor habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became more strict about leaving route plans and carrying basic emergency gear.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and neither has anyone in my immediate family. I have known acquaintances with DUIs, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Did those DUI cases affect how you think about drinking?
follow_ups.response: Yes. If I am at a beer tasting, I limit myself or make sure Megan is driving.

follow_ups.question: Was that common in your social circle?
follow_ups.response: No, but in Montana you hear enough stories that you take it seriously.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in pretty much every general election and most local elections. I started voting regularly in my twenties, and I take local races seriously because school boards, county commissioners, and judges can affect day-to-day life more than people admit. I usually read the voter guide, check local reporting, and talk with Megan, though we do not always vote the same way. I am not a sign-in-the-yard person most years, but I do vote.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually by mail, because I can sit with the ballot and do my homework.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever volunteered for a campaign?
follow_ups.response: No, not formally. I have donated small amounts to local candidates before.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as a moderate independent with a practical streak. I care about fiscal responsibility, functioning infrastructure, public lands, good schools, and personal privacy. On some issues I am probably center-left, especially health care access, environmental protection, and the idea that government has a role when markets leave people behind. On other issues I am cautious about overpromising, because I have seen organizations fail when they do not understand implementation details. Living in Montana has made public lands and local control more important to me, but I do not like performative politics from either side. I want competent government, honest budgeting, and leaders who can admit tradeoffs. I tend to trust people who have done the homework more than people who just repeat slogans.

follow_ups.question: What issues would most influence your vote locally?
follow_ups.response: Public lands, housing affordability, schools, property taxes, and whether the candidate seems competent with basic administration.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: A little, but carefully. I would rather have a useful conversation over coffee than trade cable-news lines.

follow_ups.question: Are there political views you held when younger that changed?
follow_ups.response: I used to be more reflexively skeptical of government. Now I still want accountability, but I have more respect for public institutions that quietly work.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: In recent years I have become more concerned about institutional trust and basic democratic norms. I still do not like wasteful spending, but I am less patient with people who act like all government is automatically bad. The pandemic made me see how much local public health, schools, and hospitals depend on ordinary competent administration. Climate and wildfire risk have also become more concrete to me because I spend so much time outdoors. I would not say I switched teams politically, but I am more focused on seriousness and less tolerant of outrage as a substitute for governing.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific event that shifted you?
follow_ups.response: The pandemic response and the 2020 election aftermath both did. I found myself valuing stability and facts more strongly.

follow_ups.question: Has that affected relationships?
follow_ups.response: A little with extended family. I try to keep conversations grounded in specific issues rather than national personalities.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say they affected me somewhat, maybe more intellectually than personally day to day because Livingston is not very diverse. The George Floyd murder made it impossible to pretend these were isolated complaints. I had to think about how my own experiences with police have been easier because of who I am. At the same time, I am cautious about reducing every local police officer to a national argument. I think accountability, training, and transparency matter, and I also think small communities need emergency response that people trust.

follow_ups.question: Did you discuss it at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with Claire. She pushed me to read more and not just say, 'Well, that is awful,' and move on.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you interpret news about policing?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I look for details about accountability, body cameras, union rules, and whether departments release information clearly.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issue is whether equal treatment under the law is actually equal in practice. I do not pretend to have firsthand experience with racial profiling, but enough people describe consistent patterns that it deserves serious attention. I also think data matters: stops, searches, use of force, complaints, and outcomes should be tracked and public. My software brain goes to systems and incentives. If a system produces bad outcomes repeatedly, you do not just blame one person and move on; you inspect the process.

follow_ups.question: Do you see this as a national issue, local issue, or both?
follow_ups.response: Both. The scale differs by place, but transparency and accountability are local responsibilities.

follow_ups.question: What kind of reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better data, independent review for serious incidents, de-escalation training, and clearer standards for use of force.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think I have become more aware of how easy it is for someone like me to treat race as an abstract topic. My family background had struggles, but they were mostly class and work struggles, not racial exclusion. Listening to coworkers and reading more history has made me see how housing, schools, policing, and wealth build on older patterns. I am not walking around feeling personally guilty every minute, but I do think responsibility means being honest about the record. I also think conversations go better when people can be specific instead of accusing each other in broad strokes.

follow_ups.question: What have you read or watched that influenced you?
follow_ups.response: Some long-form reporting, local public radio discussions, and history pieces about housing policy and policing.

follow_ups.question: Do your kids think differently about this than you do?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially Claire. She is more direct and less patient with gradualism.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and a few friends, and I have tried to read more. I have not joined protests, but I have supported local candidates who talk seriously about accountability and community services.

follow_ups.question: Why not protest?
follow_ups.response: Partly temperament and partly location. I am more likely to act through voting, donations, and conversations.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed anything in your volunteer work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly trying to be more aware of access issues when teaching computer basics at the library.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Megan is thoughtful about it and tends to focus on schools and fairness in public services. Claire is the most engaged and will challenge me if she thinks I am being too cautious. Owen listens more than he talks, but school discussions and online content have shaped him. My brother in Iowa is more skeptical of some activist language, though even he agrees the George Floyd case was indefensible. Among friends, there is a range, so I try to keep discussions concrete.

follow_ups.question: Have any conversations become tense?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with extended family on Facebook, which is one reason I do not argue there much.

follow_ups.question: Who influences your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: Probably Claire, because she asks direct questions and expects me to have reasons.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is good for fifty, but not perfect. I am active with hiking, fishing, skiing, and yard work, so I am not sedentary outside work. I do have borderline high blood pressure that my doctor is watching, and my knees complain after long downhill hikes. I wear glasses for reading and computer work, and I am overdue more often than I should be for dental checkups. Mentally, I do better when I have routines and time outdoors.

follow_ups.question: Are you taking medication for blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Not right now. My doctor wants me to focus on exercise, salt, weight, and monitoring first.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a year for a physical, unless something comes up.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Living here makes it easy to be active because trails and the river are close. The hard part is that software work means long sitting stretches, and winter weather can shrink the day. I also like craft beer and hearty food, so moderation takes attention. When my calendar is too full, exercise is the first thing that slips.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Walking at lunch and getting outside on weekends.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest to maintain?
follow_ups.response: Stretching and dental appointments. I always mean to schedule them.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major like surgery or a serious diagnosis. The main thing was my doctor flagging borderline blood pressure last year and telling me not to ignore it. I also had a flare-up of knee pain after a steep hike in the Gallatin range, and I had to take a few weeks off harder trails. It reminded me that I cannot treat my body like I am thirty-five. I bought better trekking poles and started doing more leg strengthening instead of just assuming hiking is enough.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee pain require imaging or specialist care?
follow_ups.response: No, just an exam and physical therapy exercises.

follow_ups.question: Did you change your diet after the blood pressure warning?
follow_ups.response: Some. Less processed lunch meat, more vegetables, and fewer second beers.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not kept me from working or parenting in any major way. Knee pain has changed some hikes, but it has not affected my job.

follow_ups.question: Have you taken sick leave recently?
follow_ups.response: Only a couple days for a winter respiratory bug.

follow_ups.question: Does computer work create any physical issues?
follow_ups.response: Neck and shoulder stiffness if I skip breaks.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My dad's mobility has become more of a concern. He has arthritis and balance issues, and because he and my mom are in Iowa, I worry from a distance. Megan had a minor skin cancer removed a few years back, and she is diligent about follow-up checks now. Nothing is a daily crisis, but there is that middle-age shift where you are watching your parents age and your kids launch at the same time. It changes the emotional background noise.

follow_ups.question: Do you help your parents with care decisions?
follow_ups.response: Some. My brother is closer physically, but I help research options and talk through finances.

follow_ups.question: Has Megan's experience changed your outdoor habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we are more serious about sunscreen and hats, especially at elevation.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I think of myself as an Independent. I am not strongly attached to either party, though in recent years I have leaned more toward Democrats in national races because of concerns about democratic norms, health care, and public lands. At the local level I will still look at the person and record. I am not allergic to voting for a Republican if they are competent, moderate, and serious about governing. Party labels matter less to me than temperament and practical judgment.

follow_ups.question: Would you call yourself a strong Independent?
follow_ups.response: Yes in the sense that I do not feel loyal to a party.

follow_ups.question: Do you split tickets?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially in local races.

follow_ups.response: Yes, if the parties changed or local candidates differed.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from identifying as a Democrat?

follow_ups.question: Was she involved in your school life?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she kept track of grades and forms.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she worked for pay most of my childhood.

follow_ups.question: Was it full time?
follow_ups.response: Mostly part time when we were young, then closer to full time later.

follow_ups.question: Did her work affect household routines?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we had chores and predictable schedules.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mom worked as a clerk and later a loan-processing assistant at a credit union. She handled customer accounts, paperwork, deposits, phone calls, and making sure forms were accurate. She was organized and patient.

follow_ups.question: Did you learn anything from watching her work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, accuracy matters and people trust you when you are steady.

follow_ups.question: Did she like the work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly. She liked helping regular people more than dealing with management changes.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: It was a local credit union. They provided savings accounts, checking, car loans, small personal loans, and basic financial services for local families and workers.

follow_ups.question: Was it a large workplace?
follow_ups.response: No, fairly small and community-oriented.

follow_ups.question: Did people in town know her through work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she often recognized people at the grocery store from the credit union.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked full time throughout my childhood.

follow_ups.question: Did he ever have layoffs?
follow_ups.response: A couple short scares, but mostly steady.

follow_ups.question: Was work central to his identity?
follow_ups.response: Very much so.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad was an industrial maintenance mechanic. He repaired equipment, handled preventive maintenance, diagnosed mechanical problems, and kept production lines running. He was the kind of person who could listen to a machine and tell something was off.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you repair skills?
follow_ups.response: Yes, basic tools, patience, and not forcing a part that does not fit.

follow_ups.question: Did that influence your software style?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Debugging code and troubleshooting machinery have more in common than people think.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked at a manufacturing plant near Dubuque that made metal components for agricultural and industrial equipment. It was loud, practical, and full of people who knew how to solve problems with their hands.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit the plant?
follow_ups.response: A couple times for family days, and I remember the noise and smell of oil.

follow_ups.question: How did that shape your view of work?
follow_ups.response: It taught me respect for maintenance, reliability, and people whose work is invisible until something breaks.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now I hope I have moved into a lead software architect role without losing touch with hands-on coding. I want to help build systems that are maintainable and useful, and I want to mentor younger developers in a way that gives them confidence and standards. I hope Megan and I are healthy, the kids are finding their footing, and my parents are getting the support they need. I want to keep living in Livingston if we can afford it and if the community still feels like a real place rather than just an expensive postcard. Personally, I want to hike the Scottish Highlands and eventually Patagonia, keep improving my woodworking, and maybe run a community tech workshop series through the library. I do not need a dramatic life. I want a durable one.

follow_ups.question: What would make the architect role satisfying?
follow_ups.response: Having enough authority to prevent avoidable problems and enough coding time to stay grounded.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope for your children?
follow_ups.response: That they become capable, kind adults who can support themselves and still make room for curiosity.

follow_ups.question: What is one concrete step toward those hopes?
follow_ups.response: Finishing the AWS certification and proposing a formal mentoring track at work.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, reliability, usefulness, and time outdoors. Reliability sounds dry, but to me it means people can count on you, your work holds up, and your promises are not decorative. I value craft too, whether it is clean code, a well-made chair, a good meal, or a careful fly cast. I value modesty and competence more than status. And I value having enough quiet in life to notice where I am.

follow_ups.question: Where did those values come from?
follow_ups.response: My parents, mostly, and years of seeing what happens when systems or people are careless.

follow_ups.question: How do you practice those values day to day?
follow_ups.response: Showing up for family, doing careful work, maintaining the house, volunteering, and making time outside.
